Which vendors actually need a 1099-NEC this year?

A private tracker for small-business bookkeepers who keep this on a spreadsheet. The 2026 reporting threshold jumped from $600 to $2,000 (OBBBA) — enter what you paid each contractor and get a sorted queue of who crosses it, who is exempt as a corporation, and whose W-9 is still missing.

After using this, you can now see exactly which vendors need a 1099-NEC and which W-9s are still missing, which used to take re-deriving the threshold rule by hand every January. See a worked example of the 2026 threshold change, how this compares to Track1099 if you are weighing a paid e-filing service, or what a hand-kept spreadsheet gets wrong if that is what you use today.

Paying yourself on a marketplace instead — Etsy, eBay, Poshmark, or similar — and reconciling a Form 1099-K you received rather than a 1099-NEC you send? The 1099-K reconciliation worksheet handles that side of the same filing season — nothing uploaded there either.

Already have the year's payments exported from your books? The 1099-NEC vendor CSV checker totals each vendor against the threshold and flags missing TINs and addresses before you file — also entirely in your browser.

Vendor names, amounts, and TINs stay on this device. Nothing is uploaded. Usage counts contain only feature names and are never sent anywhere.

Common questions

What is the 2026 1099-NEC reporting threshold, and did it really change?

Yes. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) raised the Form 1099-NEC / 1099-MISC nonemployee-compensation reporting threshold from $600 to $2,000, effective for payments made on or after January 1, 2026, with inflation adjustments starting in 2027. This tracker applies $600 to payments made before 2026 and $2,000 from 2026 on — verify the current figure in the IRS Instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC, since a later inflation adjustment can move it and this page will not know until updated. Use the threshold override above if a newer published figure applies.

Does the corporation exemption mean I never send a 1099 to an LLC or corporation?

Not always. Payments to a C-corporation, S-corporation, or an LLC taxed as a corporation are generally exempt from 1099-NEC reporting — except payments for an attorney's own fees, which are reportable regardless of the attorney's entity type. This tracker applies that exception. It does not compute two related categories that follow their own separate rules: gross proceeds paid to an attorney (1099-MISC box 10, its own $600 threshold that did not move with OBBBA) and medical or health-care payments (1099-MISC, also corp-reportable). Those show as "Check separately" rather than a guessed answer.

What does "Check separately (not calculated)" mean?

It means the category you picked follows a reporting rule this tracker has not verified closely enough to compute a threshold or deadline for. Rather than print a number that might be wrong, the row is flagged for you to check against the current IRS Instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC or your preparer.

Is the TIN check here the same as the IRS TIN Matching program?

No. The IRS TIN Matching program needs its own e-Services account and checks a name/TIN pair against IRS records — this page cannot do that on your behalf. The optional TIN field here only checks that what you typed has the shape of a Social Security Number or EIN (nine digits, in either grouping), to catch an obvious typo before it reaches a form. It never confirms the number is correct, assigned, or matches the name.

Where is my vendor data stored?

In this browser's local storage only. Nothing is uploaded to a server. Closing the tab does not lose your vendors — they are still there next time you open the page on the same device and browser.

Is this tax advice or an IRS e-filing service?

No. It is a planning tracker that turns numbers you enter into a review queue. It does not file anything with the IRS, determine your correct entity classification, or replace your tax preparer — verify every row before acting on it.

No warranty. This tool is free and as-is. It is not legal, financial, or tax advice and does not replace a qualified tax preparer. vs-track1099.html.text:
← 1099-NEC Vendor Tracker

This tracker vs. Track1099

Track1099, an Avalara product, is a well-known paid service for the back half of 1099 season: collecting W-9s from vendors electronically and e-filing 1099-NEC and 1099-MISC forms with the IRS and participating states, priced per form, described on track1099.com. It is the tool a business reaches for once it already knows its full vendor list and is ready to file.

That is a different job from the one this page does. This tracker has no W-9 collection portal, no e-filing, and no per-form fee. It exists for the step before that: working out, from what you already know about each vendor, who actually needs a 1099-NEC under the 2026 $2,000 threshold, who is exempt as a corporation, and whose W-9 is still missing — with nothing to sign up for.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I have my full 1099 list finalized — how do I collect any outstanding W-9s electronically and e-file everything with the IRS and states? Track1099 or a comparable paid e-filing service — collection and e-filing are jobs this page does not attempt.
Which of my vendors actually crosses the 2026 $2,000 threshold, and which ones are exempt because they're a corporation? This tracker — enter each vendor's entity type, category, and year-to-date total, and get the threshold and exemption applied with no signup.
Which vendors on my list still don't have a W-9 on file, so I know who to chase before the deadline? This tracker — the review queue sorts a missing W-9 above everything else and marks it done the moment you record one received.
I need audit-trail e-filing confirmations and state-by-state submission. Track1099 or a comparable paid service — this page has no accounts and files nothing; it produces a CSV you can hand to whichever service you use.

This tracker is deliberately the opposite shape from an e-filing subscription: nothing to sign up for, nothing billed per form, and nothing typed here ever leaves your browser. That makes it useful for narrowing down a vendor list before you pay anyone to file it — and the wrong tool for the actual e-filing step, which is exactly the job a service like Track1099 is built for.

It needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this tracker or Track1099?

They answer different questions. Track1099, an Avalara product, collects W-9s from vendors and e-files 1099s with the IRS and states for a per-form fee, described on Avalara's own site. This tracker does not file anything and never will — it exists for the step before that: figuring out, from what you already know about each vendor, who actually crosses the 2026 $2,000 threshold, who is exempt as a corporation, and whose paperwork is still missing. A business that already knows its full 1099 list and wants to e-file it should use Track1099 or a comparable service; a bookkeeper still working out who is even on that list is in the right place here first.

Is this page affiliated with Avalara or Track1099?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Avalara, Inc. or Track1099. Track1099 is named here only to describe what this tracker is and is not.

vs-tracking-vendors-in-a-spreadsheet.htm.text:
← 1099-NEC Vendor Tracker

This tracker vs. tracking vendors in a spreadsheet

A spreadsheet is how most small-business bookkeepers already do this, and for one filing season it can work fine: a column for total paid, a column for entity type, and an IF formula that flags a row. The problem is not the spreadsheet — it is that the formula is only as current as whoever last edited it, and two rules changed for 2026 at once.

First, the reporting threshold rose from $600 to $2,000 for payments made on or after 2026-01-01. A formula copied forward from last year's sheet still says 600 until someone remembers to change it. Second, a blanket IF(entity = "corp", "exempt", "check") rule leaves out the one case that does not follow entity type: an attorney's own fees for services are reportable no matter how the firm is organized. Getting that exception into a formula, and keeping it there through a rewrite, is easy to skip.

What a spreadsheet formula doesWhat this tracker does instead
Carries whatever threshold number was typed in last, which is often the prior year's figure until someone notices it is wrong. Applies $2,000 to payments made in 2026 or later and $600 before that, keyed to the tax year you pick — nothing to remember to update.
A blanket "corporation = exempt" rule marks every corporate-entity row exempt, including an attorney's own fees — the one category that is reportable regardless of entity type. Applies the corporation exemption except for attorney fees specifically, so a firm organized as an LLC taxed as a corporation still gets flagged for its own fee payments.
Has no place to flag "this follows a different rule I haven't encoded" — a row either matches the formula or gets a wrong answer. Routes attorney gross-proceeds and medical/health-care payments to "check separately" instead of guessing, because those follow their own box-specific rules this tracker has not verified closely enough to compute.
Tracks whether a W-9 is on file as just another column, with no ordering to say which missing one is most urgent. Sorts a missing W-9 to the top of the review queue and marks it resolved the moment you record one received.

A worked example, evaluated for tax year 2026. A $950 payment to an individual contractor, a $5,400 attorney's-fee payment to a firm organized as an LLC taxed as a corporation, and a $4,100 services payment to a C-corporation. A spreadsheet still running the pre-2026 $600 threshold flags the $950 contractor as needing a 1099 — wrong, since $950 is below the 2026 $2,000 threshold. A spreadsheet running a blanket "corporation = exempt" rule marks the $5,400 attorney payment exempt — wrong, since attorney fees are reportable regardless of entity type. This tracker reports the $950 contractor as below threshold, not yet reportable, and the $5,400 attorney payment as needing a 1099 with the W-9 on file. The $4,100 C-corp services payment is correctly exempt either way, because ordinary services to a corporation is not the exception.

It needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is ever sent anywhere.

Common questions

What does a hand-kept 1099 spreadsheet usually get wrong?

Two things, usually silently. First, its threshold formula is whatever number someone typed in last — often still $600, copied forward from a prior year, when payments made in 2026 or later use $2,000. Second, a blanket "if entity is a corporation, mark exempt" rule leaves out the one exception that does not follow entity type: an attorney's own fees for services are reportable no matter how the firm is organized. A spreadsheet formula has to encode both the threshold and the exception correctly, and re-encode the threshold again whenever it changes; this tracker applies the current rule every time.

Can you show a real example of the mismatch?

Three vendors, evaluated for 2026: a $950 payment to an individual contractor, a $5,400 attorney's-fee payment to a firm organized as an LLC taxed as a corporation, and a $4,100 payment to a C-corporation for ordinary services. A spreadsheet still using the pre-2026 $600 threshold flags the $950 contractor as needing a 1099 — wrong, since $950 is below the 2026 $2,000 threshold. A spreadsheet using a blanket "corporation = exempt" rule marks the $5,400 attorney payment exempt — wrong, since attorney fees are reportable regardless of entity type. This tracker gets both right: below threshold, not yet reportable for the first; needs a 1099, W-9 on file for the second. The $4,100 C-corp services payment is correctly exempt either way, because ordinary services to a corporation are not the exception.

Isn't a spreadsheet good enough once it's set up correctly?

It can be, for one filing season. The risk is not that a spreadsheet formula is hard to write once — it is that nothing prompts anyone to revisit it when a rule changes, the way the threshold just did. A cell holding "600" looks exactly as confident the year the real number becomes 2000 as it did the year before. This tracker has no stored formula to go stale; the threshold and the exception are applied fresh against the tax year you pick.

Does this tracker replace a spreadsheet entirely?

For deciding who needs a 1099-NEC and whose W-9 is missing, yes — that is the one job it does. It keeps no ledger of payment history, invoices, or vendor contact details beyond what you type in, and it does not e-file or generate the form itself. A bookkeeper who wants a running payment ledger across the year, not just a threshold check at filing time, still has reasons to keep a spreadsheet alongside it.

Nothing here says or implies that tracking 1099 vendors in a spreadsheet is a mistake — it is the default most small businesses already use, and it works until a rule the formula did not anticipate changes. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it. The $950, $5,400, and $4,100 figures above are this tracker's own arithmetic on the three example vendors described in this page, not a claim about any specific business's real payments.

when-do-i-need-to-send-a-1099.html.text:
← 1099-NEC Vendor Tracker

When do I actually need to send a 1099?

For payments made in 2026 and later, the answer to "did this vendor cross the threshold" changed for the first time since 1954. A vendor who was reportable at $650 in 2025 is not reportable at $650 in 2026 — and a spreadsheet built around the old $600 line will flag vendors that no longer need one, or worse, hide the habit of checking altogether.

Open the free 1099-NEC vendor tracker

What actually changed

The general threshold: $600 to $2,000. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) raised the Form 1099-NEC / 1099-MISC nonemployee-compensation reporting threshold to $2,000 for payments made on or after January 1, 2026. It will adjust for inflation starting with payments made in 2027, so treat $2,000 as the 2026 figure specifically, not a number fixed forever.

The corporation exemption did not change. A C-corp, S-corp, or LLC taxed as a corporation is still generally exempt from 1099-NEC reporting regardless of how much you paid it — except an attorney's own fees, which are reportable no matter how the firm is organized. That exception is older than the threshold change and the threshold change did not touch it.

Some related categories follow their own separate rules. Gross proceeds paid to an attorney (a settlement, for example) go on 1099-MISC box 10 under section 6045(f), which kept its own $600 threshold. Medical and health-care payments also stay reportable to a corporation. Both are different calculations from the general threshold above.

Worked example

Four vendors paid in 2026, reviewed the same afternoon:

VendorEntityPaidResult
Freelance web designerSingle-member LLC$3,200Above $2,000 — needs a 1099-NEC
One-off courier jobIndividual$450Below $2,000 — not yet reportable (would have been, under the old $600 line)
Print shopC-corporation$4,100Exempt — corporation, ordinary services
Law firm, own feesLLC taxed as a corporation$5,400Needs a 1099-NEC — attorney fees are never exempt

The courier is the row worth noticing: under the pre-2026 $600 line that vendor would have needed a form, and under the 2026 $2,000 line they don't. A vendor list built by copying last year's reportable set forward will miss that the line moved and flag someone who no longer needs a form — or, run the other direction on an older year, miss someone who does. Load the sample vendors in the tracker to see this exact queue rendered live, including the two categories the tracker flags rather than calculates.

Common questions

What changed about the 1099 threshold in 2026?

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) raised the Form 1099-NEC / 1099-MISC nonemployee-compensation reporting threshold from $600 to $2,000 for payments made on or after January 1, 2026 — the first change to that number since 1954. It will adjust for inflation starting with payments made in 2027.

Does the higher threshold mean I never have to send a 1099 to a corporation?

The corporation exemption is a separate, older rule the threshold change did not touch. Payments to a C-corp, S-corp, or an LLC taxed as a corporation are generally exempt regardless of amount — except an attorney's own fees for services, which are always reportable no matter how the firm is organized.

What about a payment I made to an attorney that isn't for the attorney's own services?

Gross proceeds paid to an attorney — for example, a settlement routed through counsel — follow a different rule, 1099-MISC box 10 under section 6045(f), with its own $600 threshold that did not move with OBBBA. That is a separate calculation from the general nonemployee-compensation threshold this page and the tracker describe.
